summary:
The Cayman Islands stands under the United Kingdom's framework. Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 2001 through an Order in Council imposed from London after the local legislature declined to act, and the reform left an unequal age of consent in its wake.

No local route to same-sex marriage exists. In March 2019 Grand Court Chief Justice Anthony Smellie struck down the statutory prohibition on same-sex marriage; the Court of Appeal overturned that ruling in August 2019 and restored the ban.

Recognition survives at the level of immigration administration. In December 2020 immigration authorities recognised the overseas same-sex marriage of Paul Pearson and Randall Pinder, who had wed in Ireland, and the Court of Appeal held that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds. An overseas marriage therefore carries immigration effects in the Cayman Islands even though no domestic route to marriage exists.

Public visibility in the tourist-facing environment is high. Around 600 people, including the premier, the governor, ministers and MLAs, joined the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation's first Pride parade on 7 August 2021, with broad official participation. Organisers asked participants to refrain from excessive displays of affection as a condition of the public-space route.
tangentialFactors:
London-local friction over the scope of protections is documented from August 2009, when the United Kingdom's Foreign Affairs Committee criticised the draft Cayman Islands constitution for deliberately excluding gay rights, calling the omission deplorable and warning that the drafting could leave the territory's courts affording citizens less protection than Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights requires. The Foreign and Commonwealth Office answered that the draft's list of discrimination grounds was open-ended.

Relationship recognition arrived through the courts and immigration administration rather than the statute book: the marriage ban was restored on appeal while the recognition-for-immigration-effects line survived. A visitor should not read the December 2020 ruling as a general marriage right.

The organisers' condition on displays of affection for the Pride route marks a public-space sensitivity that persists alongside the broad official participation recorded in 2021.
localsOnly:
Recognition of an overseas same-sex marriage in the Cayman Islands runs through immigration administration rather than a marriage statute, so its reach is tied to immigration status and the circumstances of the case before the Court of Appeal in December 2020.

The statutory ban on same-sex marriage was reinstated by the Court of Appeal in August 2019, reversing Chief Justice Smellie's March 2019 ruling, and no legislative route to marriage has been enacted since.

The constitutional list of discrimination grounds is described by the United Kingdom's foreign office as open-ended, a position taken in answer to the 2009 Foreign Affairs Committee criticism that the draft had deliberately excluded gay rights.

Unequal age of consent is a resident-facing feature of the criminal law as left by the 2001 decriminalising order.

Official participation in the August 2021 Pride parade included the premier, the governor, ministers and MLAs, indicating institutional tolerance in public visibility while organisers restricted displays of affection on the route.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains no information on legal gender recognition, the sex or gender marking on Cayman Islands identity documents, access to gender-affirming care, restroom or facility rules, or hate-crime provisions covering gender identity.

Whether the unequal age of consent left by the 2001 decriminalisation has since been harmonised is unresolved in the sources; they record the inheritance, not its current text.

Whether Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights operates as directly enforceable domestic law in the Cayman Islands is unresolved. The 2009 exchange records a committee warning about the draft's reach and a ministerial reply, not a ruling.

Enforcement data on violence against trans people, sentencing outcomes, and any trans-specific protection machinery are not sourced.
